arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Russell argued that knowing use implies knowing the specific item.
Justice Alito challenged this view with a hypothetical about a mugger.
Justice Breyer used a Denver ordinance example to test the logic.
Justice Ginsburg noted the government agrees on most elements of the statute.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests the scope of a federal identity theft statute. the side that brought the case argues the law requires knowledge of the victim. The government argues the law only requires knowledge of the document itself.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the conviction overturned. the side that brought the case argues the statute requires knowledge of the specific victim.
The government wants the conviction upheld. The government argues the statute only requires knowledge of the document.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case claims common usage implies knowing the specific item and its owner.
The government claims the statute lists specific felonies and does not require victim knowledge.

paragraphs: This case defines the mental state required for federal identity theft. It determines the scope of criminal liability for using identification documents. It affects how prosecutors charge similar offenses nationwide.
